title: Who taxes you, on what, and through whom
summary: Every tax question about a property deal reduces to three questions: which country has the right to tax, whether the profit is income or capital, and whether the vehicle pays tax itself or passes it through. Answer them in that order, before you ask about any rate.
body:
Mr Shabazz, before you ever ask what the tax rate is, answer three questions in order: who has the right to tax this profit, what kind of profit it is, and whether the vehicle pays the tax itself or passes it to its owners. Get those three right and the rate is a lookup; get them wrong and no rate will save you.

Recall

Q. What does it mean to pierce the corporate veil?

A. A court sets aside the separate legal personality of a company and holds the owners personally responsible, usually because the company was used as a sham or to commit a wrong. Limited liability is a privilege the law grants, and it can be withdrawn.

Q. What is needed to form a binding contract?

A. An offer, an acceptance that matches it, consideration or its local equivalent, an intention to be legally bound, and terms certain enough to enforce. A letter of intent may or may not bind depending on its wording.

Q. What is stabilised net operating income?

A. Net operating income (NOI) is rent and other income, less vacancy and operating expenses, before debt service and income tax. Stabilised means the figure once the building is leased up and running at its normal level.

Why this matters

Tax is usually the largest single cost on the profit of a successful development, and unlike construction cost it is set by choices you make before you break ground. The vehicle you buy the land in, where its decisions are made, and how you describe your intention when you buy all decide how the profit is taxed years later. By the time the building sells, the answer is mostly fixed. A developer who treats tax as something the accountant handles at year end is handing away a decision that belongs at the go or no-go gate.

Question one: residence versus source

In plain English: a country taxes you either because of who you are, or because of where the money was made. The first is called residence, a legal status that usually lets a country tax a person on income from anywhere in the world. The second is called source, the country where the income arises, which usually taxes only the income earned inside its borders. Real estate is the clearest case of source taxation there is: the land cannot move, so the country where it sits almost always claims a right to tax the rent and the gain.

The professional framing is that the two claims overlap. A person resident in Country A who owns a rental building in Country B may be taxed by B because the building is there, and by A because the owner lives there. Countries reduce this double tax in two main ways: the residence country gives a credit for the tax paid at source, or it exempts that income. Treaties between countries decide which applies, and we study them properly in week 57. For now, hold the principle: source has the first bite on land, residence has the last word on the person.

Applied example, hypothetical round numbers. You live in Country A and hold a building in Country B through a company incorporated in Country B. You might assume the company is resident in B because that is where it was registered. Many systems also ask where the company is actually managed and controlled. If every real decision is made at your kitchen table in Country A, the company may be resident in A as well, and both countries may treat it as theirs. Registration is a fact on paper; management is a fact about where people decide.

Question two: income versus capital

The same profit can be taxed in two very different ways depending on its character. Income is the profit of a business carried on, such as selling the units you built to sell. Capital is the gain on an asset held to produce income, such as a rental building you kept for years and then sold. Many systems tax capital gains more lightly than business income, and some treat them very differently, so the label matters.

The label is not chosen by what you call it. Authorities and courts generally look at the facts: what you intended when you bought, how long you held, whether you have done this repeatedly, how you financed it, whether you subdivided and marketed, and what your business actually is. The exact tests vary by country; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Worked example, hypothetical. Two developers each buy a lot for 1,000,000 and sell it three years later for 1,600,000, a profit of 600,000. Developer one bought it with a board resolution recording an intention to build and hold rentals, obtained a long-term mortgage, and sold only after an unsolicited offer. Developer two bought it with a short bridge loan, applied for subdivision in month two, and listed the lots with an agent. Same profit, same land, but the facts point the first toward capital and the second toward business income. If, purely as an illustration, income were taxed at twice the effective rate of capital, the difference on 600,000 is large enough to change whether the deal was worth doing.

Say that out loud now.

Question three: who pays, the vehicle or the owners

A flow-through entity is a vehicle whose profit is taxed in the hands of its owners rather than in the vehicle itself. A partnership is the classic example: it may file a return and compute its profit, but the tax is paid by the partners on their shares. A corporation is usually the opposite, a separate taxpayer that pays tax on its own profit, after which the shareholders may be taxed again when the profit is paid out as a dividend. Trusts sit in between and depend heavily on the country and the trust terms.

The choice changes three things. First, how many layers of tax there are. Second, where losses go: in a flow-through, early losses can often be used by the owners against their other income; in a corporation they usually stay inside it. Third, who must file and when. Flow-through does not mean tax-free. It means the tax moves to the owner, who may have to pay on profit that was never distributed to them in cash.

Applied example. Three investors each put in a third of the equity for a rental building. In a partnership, each reports a third of the profit on their own return, whatever their personal rate. In a corporation, the company pays tax once, and then each investor is taxed when dividends arrive. If one investor is non-resident, both structures raise separate withholding and filing questions in the source country. That is why the residence of every owner belongs on the first page of the structure memo.

How the best do it

Large institutional owners do not choose a holding vehicle and then ask what it costs in tax. They model the after-tax return for each class of investor before the land is tied up, write a short tax memo that records the intended character of the profit and the residence of every entity, and keep that memo in the deal file alongside the pro forma. Board meetings for foreign holding companies are held, minuted and attended where the company is meant to be managed. A small developer can copy all of it: one page, written before the offer, updated at each gate.

The biggest risk

Character drift. You buy saying you will hold, then behave like a trader: you subdivide, market, flip, repeat. Or you register a company abroad and then make every decision at home. In both cases the paperwork says one thing and the conduct says another, and authorities follow the conduct. The control is a written record of intention and management at acquisition, a decision log that shows where and by whom real decisions were made, and a review at each gate asking whether the facts still match the memo. Professional sign-off required: a qualified tax adviser in each country involved.

The beginner's mistake

Opening the conversation with "what is the rate?" The rate is the last fact you need, not the first. Ask who taxes, what kind of profit, and through whom; then look up the rate, and verify it against the primary source for the year in question.

Callback

In week 15 you met after-tax leakage: the gap between the return a deal earns and the return its owners keep. This lesson is where that leakage begins. And in week 21 you learned that limited liability can be lost when a company is used as a mere instrument of its owner. Tax authorities reason in a similar way about residence: a company that has no mind of its own, because its owner decides everything elsewhere, may be treated as living where the owner lives. Both rules punish the same habit, a structure that exists only on paper.

Recap

Three questions, in order. Residence versus source decides which country taxes. Income versus capital decides the character of the profit, and facts decide it, not labels. Flow-through versus separate taxpayer decides how many layers there are and who pays. Write the answers down before you sign anything. Rates come last and are always verified against the primary source.

Next: Ford, Failure Forensics, on a trust that was registered in one country and found to live in another.
checklist: Write down the residence of every owner and every entity before choosing a structure
Note where each entity's real decisions will be made, and by whom
Record your intention for the asset at acquisition: build to sell, or build to hold
List the facts that could make the profit income rather than capital
Decide whether each vehicle pays tax itself or passes it to owners, and why
Check where early losses will go in the chosen vehicle
Ask a qualified tax adviser in each country to confirm the analysis in writing
Look up rates last, and verify them against the primary source for that year
head: Field checklist
speak: Every tax question about a deal comes down to three questions, asked in order. First, who has the right to tax this profit. A country taxes because of where you live, called residence, or because of where the money was made, called source. Land cannot move, so the country where the building sits nearly always claims the first bite. Second, what kind of profit is it. Business income and capital gains are often taxed very differently, and the facts decide which it is, not the label you put on it: your intention at purchase, how long you held, how you financed it and how often you do this. Third, through whom. A partnership usually passes its profit to the partners, who pay the tax. A corporation pays its own tax, then shareholders may pay again on dividends. Answer those three before you ask about a rate, and verify every rate against the primary source.
terms: Residence — the legal status that usually lets a country tax a person or company on income from anywhere in the world
Source — the country where income arises, which usually taxes only the income earned inside its borders
Flow-through entity — a vehicle whose profit is taxed in the hands of its owners rather than in the vehicle itself

hostile.q: Your company is incorporated abroad, but you live here and you sign everything. Why shouldn't we treat it as resident here?
hostile.a: That is the right question, and the answer has to be in the record, not in my assurance. The board meets and decides where the company is registered, the minutes show who attended and where, and the decisions you see in the file were made there. If the record does not show that, then you may well be right, and I would rather know now and restructure than defend a position the facts do not support.

role: Failure forensics, with Cole (Audit and integrity)
title: The trust that lived where its decisions were made
summary: In the Fundy Settlement case, decided by the Supreme Court of Canada in 2012, trusts with a trustee in Barbados were held to be resident in Canada because the real decisions were made there. The lesson for a developer is that residence follows conduct, and an address cannot carry it.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a company or trust lives where its real decisions are made, not where its letterhead says it lives. The Fundy Settlement case is the clearest proof Canada has, and the mistake at its heart is one any developer with a foreign holding company can make.

Recall

Q. What is a personal guarantee, and why does it matter after a breach?

A. A personal guarantee makes the owner personally liable for a company's debt. When a covenant breaks, the lender can call it, which removes the protection of limited liability for that debt.

Q. In failure forensics, what is the point of no return?

A. The moment after which the outcome could no longer be avoided at reasonable cost. Finding it tells you when a warning still mattered.

Q. What is lease-up, and why does it carry risk?

A. Lease-up is the period between completion and stabilisation when units are being let. It carries risk because carrying costs run while income is still building, and slow absorption stretches the gap.

Why this matters

Developers who invest across borders often hold property through a company or trust set up in another country, sometimes for good commercial reasons and sometimes for tax. Either way, the structure only works if the entity really is resident where it claims to be. This case shows what happens when the paperwork says one place and the conduct says another. Cole is with me today because the evidence, not the theory, decided it. The broad facts below are drawn from the published judgments; verify the details against them before you rely on any of them.

Step 1: Timeline

Late 1990s: trusts were settled as part of the reorganisation of a family-owned Canadian business group, with a trust company in Barbados appointed as trustee. Around 2000: the trusts sold shares in Canadian companies to an unrelated buyer and realised a large gain. The trusts took the position that they were resident in Barbados and that the tax treaty between Canada and Barbados exempted the gain from Canadian tax. The Canadian tax authority disagreed and assessed. 2009: the Tax Court of Canada held that the trusts were resident in Canada. 2010: the Federal Court of Appeal agreed. 2012: the Supreme Court of Canada agreed, in the case reported as Fundy Settlement v. Canada, sometimes cited under the trustee's name, St. Michael Trust Corp.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. The decision to appoint an offshore trustee and rely on its address for residence. The decision, in practice, to leave substantive control with the Canadian-resident beneficiaries who were also the business owners. And the decision to claim the treaty exemption on the sale.

Step 3: Assumptions

The core assumption was that a trust is resident where its trustee resides. That was a reasonable reading of older authority, which is exactly why it was dangerous. The courts held that the test for a trust should follow the test long used for companies: central management and control, meaning the place where the highest-level strategic decisions are actually made. Where the trustee merely carried out decisions made by others, the trustee's address did not decide residence.

Step 4: Incentives

The tax at stake on a large gain created a powerful incentive to adopt the structure. The advisers who designed it were paid for it. The trustee was paid to act, and a trustee paid a modest fee to administer has little reason to insist on making hard decisions itself. Nobody in that chain was paid to ask the uncomfortable question: who really decides?

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The trial court found that the main beneficiaries, living in Canada, made the substantive decisions and that the trustee's role was limited in practice. In any structure like this, the warning signs are visible to anyone who looks: the offshore director or trustee never says no, signs documents prepared elsewhere, has no independent advice, and meets the owners only when a signature is needed. Emails show decisions taken at home and ratified abroad afterwards.

Step 6: Point of no return

Residence is judged on what happened, so the point of no return was not the court hearing. It was the period before and during the sale, when the real decisions about the shares were made in Canada. Once those facts existed, no later paperwork could change where the trusts had been managed.

Step 7: Root cause

Treating residence as a fact on paper instead of a fact about conduct. The structure placed the address in one country and left the mind of the trust in another.

The developer's version

This is a hypothetical composite, not the case. A developer incorporates a holding company abroad to own shares of a project company at home. He appoints a local nominee director. Every decision on financing, the contractor and the sale is made by him at home and sent abroad to be signed. Years later, a sale produces a large gain. The tax authority at home asks for the board minutes, the emails and the travel records. They show the developer decided everything at home. The foreign company may be treated as resident at home, and the planned result fails, with interest added.

Cole's evidence check

Cole's point is that residence cases are won and lost on documents most people never think of as tax documents. If an authority questions where an entity is managed, expect it to ask for board and trustee minutes, the briefing papers sent before each meeting, emails and messages about the decisions, travel and calendar records showing who was where, the engagement letters of the people who drafted the documents, and evidence of whether the offshore director or trustee ever asked a question, sought advice or refused a request. It will compare the dates: if the email agreeing a sale price at home predates the foreign meeting that approved it, the meeting looks like ratification, not decision.

Apply this to yourself, hypothetically. Picture your own inbox for the last month and ask: if a stranger read only these messages, where would they say my companies are managed? If the honest answer is "wherever I am," then the companies are managed wherever you are, and the structure should be designed on that basis rather than against it.

What would have changed the outcome

Not cleverer drafting. A trustee with real authority, real information and a real willingness to decide, meeting where it was resident, would have given the structure substance. That costs money and, more importantly, it costs control: the owners must actually let someone else decide. Many structures fail at exactly that point, because the owner wants the tax result of giving up control without giving it up.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is not a bad structure; it is a good structure run badly. The control is a substance record: board meetings held where the entity is meant to be managed, attended by directors or trustees who have the information and authority to decide, minutes that show real deliberation, and a decision log that would survive a hostile reading. Professional sign-off required: a tax adviser in each country, and a corporate lawyer for the governance.

The beginner's mistake

Believing the structure diagram. A diagram shows ownership. It says nothing about where decisions happen, and residence is about decisions.

Rule 22

Rule 22: Residence follows the decisions, not the address. If the decisions are made here, no paperwork will move them there.

Callback

Three lessons ago, in week 21, the question was when a court will set aside a company's separate existence. Courts look past form to what actually happened. Fundy is the tax version of the same discipline. And in week 2 you learned to keep a decision journal; here the decision journal is not a self-improvement tool but evidence, because where and by whom a decision was made can decide which country taxes the result.

Recap

Offshore trustee, onshore decisions, large gain, treaty claim, three courts, one answer: resident where central management and control actually sat. The structure failed on conduct, not drafting. Rule 22 is the prevention: put decisions where the entity lives, and keep the evidence.

Next: Sage, The Money, on how character and vehicle change your after-tax return.
checklist: For every entity, name the place it is meant to be managed
Confirm its directors or trustees can and do make real decisions
Hold board meetings where the entity is meant to be managed, and minute them properly
Keep a decision log: what was decided, by whom, where and when
Make sure emails do not show decisions taken elsewhere and ratified later
Brief offshore directors with the information they need to say no
Get written advice in each country before relying on a treaty position
head: Field checklist
speak: In the Fundy Settlement case, decided by the Supreme Court of Canada in 2012, family trusts appointed a trustee in Barbados and then sold shares of Canadian companies at a large gain. They claimed they lived in Barbados and that a tax treaty exempted the gain. Three Canadian courts disagreed. The test for where a trust lives is where its central management and control actually sits, and on the facts, the substantive decisions were made by beneficiaries in Canada while the trustee mostly carried them out. So the trusts were resident in Canada and the exemption failed. The root cause was treating residence as a fact on paper instead of a fact about conduct. For a developer with a foreign holding company, the lesson is direct. Residence follows the decisions, not the address. Hold real meetings where the entity lives, with directors who can say no, and keep the record.
terms: Central management and control — the place where an entity's highest-level strategic decisions are actually made, used to decide where it is resident
Treaty exemption — relief under a tax treaty that removes one country's right to tax an item of income
Substance record — the evidence showing that an entity is genuinely managed where it claims to be

hostile.q: Your holding company's director lives abroad. Show me one decision that director made that you did not make first.
hostile.a: I will show you the minutes and the briefing papers for the meetings where the financing and the sale were decided, including the meeting where the director asked for a further valuation before approving. If I cannot show you decisions made there by people with the authority to make them, then you should not accept the residence claim, and neither should I.

rule: Rule 22: Residence follows the decisions, not the address. If the decisions are made here, no paperwork will move them there.

title: What tax character does to your return
summary: The same building can deliver very different returns depending on whether the profit is taxed as income or capital and whether the vehicle pays tax itself or passes it through. This lesson puts numbers on that difference and shows why the after-tax return is the only one you can spend.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the return in the pro forma is a pre-tax number, and you cannot spend a pre-tax number. Character and vehicle can move your equity multiple by more than a good contractor saves you, so they belong in the model from the first draft.

Recall

Q. When someone across the table says a fixed price is final, what is the question behind it?

A. Usually not the price itself but certainty: they want to know you will close, or they are protecting a number they have already promised someone else. Ask what would make them comfortable before you move on price.

Q. What is consideration in contract law?

A. Something of value given by each party in exchange for the other's promise. Without it, in systems that require it, a promise is generally not enforceable as a contract.

Q. What does vacancy allowance do in a pro forma?

A. It reduces potential gross income by an assumed percentage for units that will be empty or not paying, so the model does not assume a full building every day of the year.

Why this matters

You will compare deals on internal rate of return (IRR), the discount rate at which the present value of the cash flows equals zero, and on the equity multiple, total cash returned divided by equity invested. Both are normally computed before tax. Two deals with the same pre-tax IRR can leave you with very different amounts of money if one produces capital gain and the other business income, or if one is held in a flow-through vehicle and the other in a corporation. If you rank deals on pre-tax numbers, you may choose the worse one.

Character changes the exit cheque

Every rate below is hypothetical and chosen for arithmetic, not reality; verify any real rate against the primary source before you rely on it.

Worked example one. You invest 2,000,000 of equity in a rental building. Ignore interim cash flow to keep it clean. In year 5 the building is sold and, after repaying the loan, 3,000,000 comes back to equity. The pre-tax gain is 1,000,000 and the pre-tax equity multiple is 3,000,000 divided by 2,000,000, which is 1.5 times. The pre-tax IRR over five years is about 8.4 percent, because 1.5 to the power of one fifth is about 1.084.

Now apply tax to the gain. Suppose, hypothetically, that capital gains bear an effective rate of 20 percent and business income 40 percent.

  1. Taxed as capital: tax is 1,000,000 times 20 percent, which is 200,000. You keep 2,800,000. Multiple 1.4 times. IRR about 7.0 percent.
  2. Taxed as income: tax is 1,000,000 times 40 percent, which is 400,000. You keep 2,600,000. Multiple 1.3 times. IRR about 5.4 percent.

Same building, same buyer, same price. The difference between the two characters is 200,000 of cash and about one and a half points of IRR, decided by facts that were mostly fixed on the day you bought the land.

Say that out loud now.

The vehicle changes the yearly cheque

Worked example two, hypothetical. The building produces 100,000 a year of taxable profit after interest and depreciation. You own all of it.

  1. Flow-through: the 100,000 is taxed on your personal return. At a hypothetical personal rate of 45 percent, tax is 45,000, leaving 55,000, whether or not the cash was paid out to you.
  2. Corporation that pays everything out: the company pays tax at a hypothetical 25 percent, which is 25,000, leaving 75,000. It pays you a dividend of 75,000, taxed at a hypothetical 30 percent, which is 22,500. You keep 52,500.
  3. Corporation that retains the profit: the company pays 25,000 and keeps 75,000 to reinvest. Nothing more is paid until you take the money out.

The lesson is not that one vehicle wins. It is that the answer depends on whether you need the cash now, how long you will leave it inside, and what the rates actually are. The third line shows deferral: tax postponed is money you can invest in the meantime, and the value of deferral grows with time and with your reinvestment return. Deferral is not exemption; the second layer is waiting.

Losses and timing

Early years of a development often produce losses or very small profits. In a flow-through vehicle, those losses may reach the owners and shelter other income, which is worth money now. In a corporation they are usually trapped until the company earns profit. If your investors have other income and want early losses, that points one way; if they want a single layer of corporate tax on retained profit to fund the next project, that points another. The model should show both, side by side, in after-tax cash flow per investor.

Putting it in the model

A clean way to show this to a partner or a lender is a two-by-two table of after-tax equity multiple, using the hypothetical numbers above and assuming every dollar is paid out at exit.

AssumptionTaxed as capitalTaxed as income
Flow-through, one layer1.40 times1.30 times
Corporation, then dividendlower againlower again

The bottom row is deliberately not filled in with a number, because the second layer depends on the dividend treatment in the relevant country and on how long the cash stays inside. That is the honest way to present it: fill in what you know, and mark what an adviser must supply. A table that shows false precision invites a partner to rely on it.

Notice what the table makes visible. The spread between the best and worst cells is driven by decisions you control: how you buy, how you behave, what vehicle you use. That is why tax belongs at the go or no-go gate, beside land price and construction cost, and not in the closing checklist.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet. When you list a property you own, the market value is not what you own; you own the market value minus the debt minus the tax that would be due if you sold. That last item is a deferred tax liability, the tax built into an asset's unrealised gain. A building worth 3,000,000 against a tax cost of 2,000,000 carries a hypothetical tax of 200,000 to 400,000 depending on character. Show it as a line. A balance sheet without it overstates your wealth, and every decision about borrowing, gifting or selling will be made on a number that is too high.

One more habit for the model: put every tax rate in a single, clearly labelled input cell marked "provisional, verify", and never type a rate directly into a formula. When the adviser confirms the real figure, you change one cell and the whole model updates, and anyone reviewing it can see in seconds which numbers were assumptions.

The biggest risk

Comparing deals on pre-tax IRR and assuming tax will be roughly the same for each. It rarely is. The control is a single row in every pro forma, after-tax cash to each class of investor, with the character and vehicle assumptions written beside it and reviewed by a qualified tax adviser before the go decision. Professional sign-off required: a tax adviser in each relevant country.

The beginner's mistake

Applying one tax rate to the whole profit. A sale often contains several kinds of profit at once, and a holding period often contains losses, profits and deferral. One blended rate hides every decision that matters.

Callback

In week 15 you learned the traps in IRR: it rewards speed, it can mislead on small deals, and it ignores leakage. Tax is the biggest leakage of all. And yesterday's case showed that the facts behind the assumption, not the assumption itself, decide the answer. A model that says "taxed as capital" is only as good as the conduct that will support it.

Recap

Character changed the exit cheque by 200,000 on a 1,000,000 gain. The vehicle changed the yearly cheque and the timing of tax. Deferral has value but is not exemption. Your balance sheet should carry the tax built into every asset. All rates here were hypothetical; verify real ones against the primary source.

Next: Omar, The Rules, on how flow-through entities actually work in law.
checklist: Add an after-tax cash flow row for each class of investor to every pro forma
Write the character assumption, income or capital, beside the exit line
Model the vehicle choice both ways when the answer is not obvious
Separate deferral from exemption in your notes
Show where early losses go and whether investors can use them
Carry a deferred tax liability line on your personal balance sheet
Have a tax adviser review the assumptions before the go decision
head: Field checklist
speak: The return in a pro forma is a pre-tax number, and you cannot spend it. Take a hypothetical deal: 2,000,000 of equity returns 3,000,000 in year five, a 1,000,000 gain, 1.5 times the money, about 8.4 percent IRR. If the gain is taxed as capital at a hypothetical 20 percent, you keep 2,800,000. If it is taxed as business income at a hypothetical 40 percent, you keep 2,600,000. That is 200,000 of real cash and a point and a half of IRR, decided by facts mostly fixed when you bought the land. The vehicle matters too. A flow-through puts the profit on your own return each year. A corporation pays its own tax, and you pay again when you take a dividend, but retained profit is deferred. Deferral has value, but it is not exemption. Put after-tax cash per investor in every model, and verify every real rate.
terms: Internal rate of return (IRR) — the discount rate at which the present value of a project's cash flows equals zero
Deferral — postponing a tax to a later date, which has value because the money can be invested in the meantime
Deferred tax liability — the tax built into an asset's unrealised gain, payable if the asset were sold

hostile.q: Your pro forma shows a 16 percent IRR. Is that before or after tax, and whose tax?
hostile.a: Before tax at the project level. Below it is the after-tax cash for each investor class, with the character and vehicle assumptions stated, and a note of what changes if the gain were taxed as income. The adviser's review of those assumptions is in the appendix. If you want one number to compare, use the after-tax row for your own class.

title: Flow-through entities: what the law says and what it doesn't
summary: A flow-through entity moves the tax to its owners, but the legal form and the tax treatment are two separate questions, and countries do not always agree on either. This lesson covers partnerships, allocations, tax distributions and hybrid mismatches in concept.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the legal form of an entity and its tax treatment are two separate questions, and you must answer both. A vehicle can be a partnership in law and a taxpayer in one country, transparent in another, and the gap between them is where most of the surprises live.

Recall

Q. Why can a limited partner lose limited liability?

A. In many systems a limited partner who takes part in managing the business may be treated as a general partner and lose the protection. The exact rule varies; verify it against the primary source.

Q. Is a letter of intent binding?

A. It depends on the words. Many letters of intent are drafted as non-binding except for specific clauses such as confidentiality, exclusivity and costs. If it is silent or ambiguous, a court may find more of it binding than you intended.

Q. What is absorption, and how is it expressed?

A. The rate at which a market takes up new supply, expressed as units leased or sold per month. It drives the length of lease-up and therefore carrying cost.

Why this matters

Most joint ventures for a rental building end up as a partnership, a limited partnership or a company that elects or is deemed to be transparent for tax. If you sign the agreement without understanding how the tax flows, you may promise investors cash they will need just to pay tax on profit they never received, or you may lose the very losses the structure was meant to deliver.

Two questions, not one

First, what is the entity in law? A general partnership is a relationship between persons carrying on business together; in many systems it has no separate legal personality and every general partner is liable for its debts. A limited partnership has at least one general partner with unlimited liability and limited partners whose liability is capped at their contribution. A corporation is a separate legal person. Second, how is it taxed? A partnership is usually transparent: the partnership computes the profit, and the partners pay the tax. A corporation is usually opaque: it pays its own tax.

These two answers can come apart. Some countries let certain entities elect their tax classification; the United States, for example, has an elective classification regime often called "check the box". Some countries tax certain partnerships as companies. A hybrid entity is one treated as transparent by one country and opaque by another. Many countries now have anti-hybrid rules aimed at mismatches that produce a deduction in one place without income in the other. Verify each against the primary source before you rely on it.

The allocation clause and the tax distribution clause

In a flow-through, the agreement decides how profit and loss are shared for tax. That is the allocation: the share of taxable profit or loss assigned to each partner. Tax authorities usually require that allocations follow the real economic arrangement and are not shuffled simply to put losses where they are most valuable. The rules on what is acceptable vary by country and are technical; this is adviser territory.

Applied example, hypothetical. Three partners own a building: A with 50 percent, B with 30 percent, C with 20 percent. The building earns 400,000 of taxable profit in a year, but every dollar of cash goes to repaying loan principal, which is not deductible. The partnership distributes nothing. Each partner is still taxed on their share: A on 200,000, B on 120,000, C on 80,000. This is phantom income, taxable profit with no cash to pay the tax. The protection is a tax distribution clause: the agreement requires the partnership, where it lawfully can, to distribute at least enough cash for partners to pay the tax on their allocated profit, at an assumed rate. Lenders often restrict distributions, so the clause must be reconciled with the loan covenants before signing.

Say that out loud now.

Who files, who is liable, who controls the audit

A flow-through usually files an information return even though it pays no tax. Someone must be responsible for preparing it, sending each partner their share, and dealing with the tax authority if the partnership's return is reviewed. Some systems now assess certain partnerships at the entity level after an audit, or designate a partner to represent all partners. Your agreement should name that person, set what they may concede without consent, and require them to share correspondence promptly.

Applied example, hypothetical. The partnership's return is reviewed and the authority proposes to reclassify a sale as business income rather than capital. The general partner, who is also the developer, earns a fee whatever the character; the limited partners bear the tax. A well-drafted agreement requires notice to all partners, gives them a say on settlement, and stops the representative conceding on character without consent. A poorly drafted one lets one person settle everyone's tax.

Non-resident partners

When a partner is non-resident, the source country may require the partnership to withhold tax on that partner's share, may require filings from the partner, or may treat the partnership differently for that partner. A non-resident partner may also face tax at home on the same profit, with relief depending on that country's rules and any treaty. None of these conclusions can be drawn without the specific countries' rules. The structural point is simple: ask about every partner's residence before agreeing the vehicle.

Trusts and other in-between vehicles

Trusts are the hardest to generalise. A trust is not usually a separate legal person; it is a relationship in which a trustee holds property for beneficiaries. For tax, some systems tax the trust as if it were a person on income it keeps, and tax beneficiaries on income paid or made payable to them, so the trust behaves partly as a flow-through and partly as a taxpayer. The terms of the trust, the residence of the trustee and the place where it is really managed all matter, as Ford showed yesterday. We study trusts properly in weeks 90 and 91; for now, treat any trust in a structure as a question for a specialist.

Five clauses to read before signing

  1. The allocation clause: does it follow the economic deal?
  2. The tax distribution clause: what assumed rate, and is it subordinate to the lender?
  3. The tax representative clause: who deals with the authority, and with what limits?
  4. The withholding clause: who bears tax withheld on a non-resident partner's share?
  5. The transfer clause: does a partner's exit trigger tax for anyone else?

The biggest risk

A mismatch between the agreement and the tax law: an allocation the authority will not respect, a promise of distributions the loan prohibits, or a hybrid entity that produces double tax instead of single tax. The control is to have the partnership agreement, the loan agreement and a written tax analysis reviewed together, by people who have read all three. Professional sign-off required: a corporate lawyer and a tax adviser, in each country where a partner or the property sits.

The beginner's mistake

Saying "it's a partnership, so there is no tax." There is tax; it simply lands on the partners, and it lands whether or not they received any cash.

Callback

In week 20 you learned that the words of an agreement decide what binds. Here the words decide something more expensive: who bears the tax and who controls the fight with the authority. And in week 21 you saw that a limited partner who manages can lose the limit. Taking part in tax settlement decisions is a governance right, so draft it carefully: protecting your tax position should not cost you your liability shield.

Recap

Legal form and tax treatment are separate questions. Partnerships usually pass profit through, which creates phantom income when cash is used to repay principal. Allocation and tax distribution clauses carry the money. Name who files and who controls an audit. Ask every partner's residence first. Verify every rule against the primary source.

Next: Nadia, The Numbers, working backward from a tax bill to the transaction that caused it.
checklist: Answer the legal form question and the tax treatment question separately
Check whether any entity is treated differently in two countries
Read the allocation clause against the real economic deal
Include a tax distribution clause, and reconcile it with the loan covenants
Name who files the partnership return and who represents the partners in an audit
Require consent before anyone concedes on character or settles a dispute
List every partner's residence before choosing the vehicle
head: Field checklist
speak: Every entity raises two separate questions: what is it in law, and how is it taxed. A partnership is usually transparent for tax, so the partners pay on their share of the profit. That creates a trap. If the building earns taxable profit but every dollar of cash goes to repaying principal, which is not deductible, the partners still owe tax on profit they never received. That is phantom income. The fix is a tax distribution clause, checked against the loan covenants, because lenders often restrict distributions. The agreement must also name who files, who deals with the tax authority, and what they may concede without consent. Beware hybrid entities, transparent in one country and opaque in another, and ask every partner's residence before choosing the vehicle. Get the lawyer and the tax adviser to read the partnership agreement, the loan and the tax analysis together.
terms: Hybrid entity — a vehicle treated as transparent by one country and as a separate taxpayer by another
Phantom income — taxable profit allocated to an owner who received no cash to pay the tax
Tax distribution clause — a provision requiring a flow-through entity to distribute enough cash for owners to pay tax on their allocated profit

hostile.q: As a limited partner, I'll be taxed on profit you use to pay down the loan. Why should I accept that?
hostile.a: You shouldn't accept it without protection. The agreement includes a tax distribution clause at a stated assumed rate, and we negotiated the loan so those distributions are permitted. Where the lender blocks a distribution, the shortfall is tracked and paid first when cash is free. You also have consent rights before anyone settles a tax dispute that changes the character of your profit.

title: Working backward from a tax bill
summary: Starting from a finished outcome, an investor's tax bill and an after-tax target, this lesson works backward to the transaction and the pre-tax profit that produced it. Reverse engineering exposes the assumptions a forward model hides.
body:
Mr Shabazz, today we start at the end. When you can take a tax bill, or an after-tax target, and work backward to the transaction behind it, you understand the structure; when you can only work forward, you understand the spreadsheet.

Recall

Q. What are the three questions to ask before any tax rate?

A. Who has the right to tax the profit, residence or source; what kind of profit it is, income or capital; and through whom, a vehicle that pays tax itself or one that passes it through.

Q. What makes a breach of contract material?

A. A breach that goes to the root of the contract and substantially deprives the other party of what they bargained for. It may allow the innocent party to terminate, not just claim damages.

Q. What is the difference between potential and effective gross income?

A. Potential gross income assumes every unit is let at full rent. Effective gross income deducts vacancy and credit loss from it.

Why this matters

Investors, partners and auditors will hand you outcomes and ask how they happened. A partner receives a tax bill for a year with no distributions. A seller says he needs a certain amount after tax. A lender asks why the company owes tax while showing a loss in its management accounts. Each is a puzzle you solve backward. All rates and figures in this lesson are hypothetical, chosen for clean arithmetic; verify real rates against the primary source before you rely on them.

Worked example one: the angry partner

The finished outcome: partner C, who owns 30 percent of a partnership that holds a rental building, received a personal tax bill of 60,000 for last year. The partnership distributed nothing. C wants to know why.

  1. Start from the bill. Assume C's personal rate on this income is a hypothetical 40 percent. Taxable income allocated to C equals 60,000 divided by 0.40, which is 150,000.
  2. C owns 30 percent and the allocation follows ownership. Partnership taxable profit equals 150,000 divided by 0.30, which is 500,000.
  3. Now find the profit in the building. Suppose rent less operating expenses, the net operating income (NOI), was 1,100,000. Deductible interest was 450,000. Depreciation deducted for tax was 150,000. 1,100,000 minus 450,000 minus 150,000 equals 500,000. That matches.
  4. Find the cash. Cash after interest equals 1,100,000 minus 450,000, which is 650,000. Depreciation is a deduction, not a payment, so it uses no cash. Suppose loan principal repaid was 600,000 and a capital repair reserve took 50,000. 650,000 minus 600,000 minus 50,000 equals zero cash to distribute.

So the answer to C: the building made 500,000 of taxable profit, C's 30 percent share is 150,000, and the cash that would have paid the tax went to principal, which is not deductible. The agreement had no tax distribution clause. The check figure that ties it together is that taxable profit, 500,000, plus depreciation, 150,000, equals cash before principal and reserve, 650,000.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two: the seller's number

The finished outcome: a landowner tells you he will sell only if he keeps 1,000,000 after tax. You want to know what price that implies, because it tells you whether his number is real or a negotiating anchor.

  1. If his gain is capital, at a hypothetical effective rate of 20 percent, the pre-tax gain he needs is 1,000,000 divided by 0.80, which is 1,250,000.
  2. If his gain is business income, at a hypothetical 40 percent, he needs 1,000,000 divided by 0.60, which is about 1,666,667.
  3. His tax cost in the land, the adjusted cost base, meaning what he paid plus allowable additions, is 400,000. Selling costs are 50,000.
  4. Required price on the capital assumption: 1,250,000 plus 400,000 plus 50,000 equals 1,700,000.
  5. Required price on the income assumption: 1,666,667 plus 400,000 plus 50,000 equals about 2,116,667.

The gap is about 416,667, and it comes entirely from the seller's own tax character, which he may not have thought about. A conversation about his position, through his own adviser, may move him more than a conversation about your feasibility. You do not advise him on his tax; you ask him whether his number is before or after tax, and on what assumption.

Worked example three: the gross-up

The finished outcome: you want each of your investors to receive 70,000 after tax next year from a flow-through vehicle. What taxable profit must be distributed? If their assumed rate is a hypothetical 30 percent, the distribution must be 70,000 divided by 0.70, which is 100,000 per investor. That is a gross-up: increasing a payment so that the after-tax amount equals a target. Gross-ups compound when the payment itself is taxable, so always divide by one minus the rate; never add the rate on top.

Worked example four: the lender's puzzle

The finished outcome: a lender sees that your project company shows a loss of 50,000 in its management accounts but paid 62,500 of income tax. It asks how a company that lost money owes tax.

  1. Start from the tax. At a hypothetical corporate rate of 25 percent, taxable profit equals 62,500 divided by 0.25, which is 250,000.
  2. The gap between taxable profit and accounting result is 250,000 minus negative 50,000, which is 300,000.
  3. Find the item. The accounts include a 300,000 provision for an expected legal settlement. Accounting rules require recognising a probable liability when it can be estimated; tax rules in many systems allow a deduction only when the amount is actually paid or becomes fixed. Verify the rule in the relevant country against the primary source.
  4. Tie out: accounting loss of negative 50,000 plus the non-deductible provision of 300,000 equals taxable profit of 250,000.

This is a timing difference: when the settlement is paid next year, the deduction arrives and the tax falls. Explaining it in one sentence, with the tie-out figure ready, turns a lender's suspicion into confidence. Nadia's habit is to keep a short reconciliation from accounting profit to taxable profit in every year-end pack, so the question never needs to be asked.

A routine for any backward problem

  1. Write the outcome exactly as stated, with its units and the date it relates to.
  2. Write every assumption you need to reverse it: rate, share, character, period.
  3. Reverse one step at a time, dividing where the forward step multiplied.
  4. Rebuild the transaction that would produce the intermediate figure.
  5. Find a tie-out figure that connects two independent calculations.
  6. State which assumption, if wrong, would change the answer most, and get it verified.

Step six is the one people skip, and it is the one that tells you where to spend your adviser's time.

The biggest risk

Accepting someone's outcome without rebuilding it. A partner's tax bill, a seller's required number or an investor's yield target can each hide an assumption about rate, character or timing that is wrong. The control is to rebuild every outcome from the transaction up, with a tie-out figure that proves the arithmetic, and to get each party's own adviser to confirm their side. Professional sign-off required: each party's own tax adviser.

The beginner's mistake

Grossing up by multiplying instead of dividing. Adding 30 percent to 70,000 gives 91,000, and 30 percent tax on 91,000 leaves 63,700, not 70,000. Divide by 0.70.

Callback

Week 17 was reverse engineering a deal from public information: implied land price, rent and return. This is the same skill applied to tax. And last week, you learned to read the words of a contract for what they actually bind. The tax distribution clause that partner C never had is the contract that would have answered his question before he asked it.

Recap

Partner C's 60,000 bill came from 500,000 of taxable profit that went to principal. The seller's 1,000,000 after tax needed a price between 1,700,000 and about 2,116,667 depending on his character. A gross-up divides by one minus the rate. Rebuild every outcome from the transaction up, and verify the rates.

Next: JAX, The Room, choosing a vehicle with two partners and their accountant.
checklist: Rebuild any tax bill from the transaction up before discussing it
Find the tie-out: taxable profit plus non-cash deductions equals cash before principal
Ask whether every target number is before or after tax, and on what assumption
Compute required prices under both income and capital assumptions
Gross up by dividing by one minus the rate, never by adding the rate
Label every rate as hypothetical until verified against the primary source
Send each party to their own adviser for their own tax position
head: Field checklist
speak: Reverse engineering a tax outcome means starting from the answer and working back to the transaction. A partner owning 30 percent receives a 60,000 tax bill and no cash. At a hypothetical 40 percent rate, his share of taxable profit was 150,000, so the partnership earned 500,000. Net operating income of 1,100,000, less 450,000 interest and 150,000 depreciation, gives 500,000. The cash went to 600,000 of principal and a 50,000 reserve, so nothing was distributed. Principal is not deductible. That is phantom income. Second, a seller wants 1,000,000 after tax. As a capital gain at a hypothetical 20 percent, he needs 1,250,000 before tax; with a 400,000 cost and 50,000 selling costs, the price is 1,700,000. As business income at 40 percent, it is about 2,116,667. And when you gross up, divide by one minus the rate. Never add the rate on top.
terms: Adjusted cost base — the tax cost of an asset, generally what was paid plus allowable additions, used to compute a gain
Gross-up — increasing a payment so that the amount left after tax equals a target
Tie-out — a check figure that proves two calculations agree

hostile.q: You told me this partnership would pay me a return. Instead I got a tax bill and no cheque. Explain it in two sentences.
hostile.a: The building earned 500,000 of taxable profit, your 30 percent share is 150,000, and the cash that would have paid your tax went to repaying loan principal, which is not deductible. We should have had a tax distribution clause, and I am proposing we add one now and reconcile it with the lender before next year.

title: Choosing the vehicle at the table
summary: A scene: two prospective joint-venture partners and their accountant meet to choose a holding vehicle, and one partner is non-resident. The lines to say, the lines never to say, and the question behind the question.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the meeting where partners choose a vehicle is not a tax meeting; it is a meeting about what each person needs, disguised as a tax meeting. Ask the needs first, and the vehicle almost chooses itself.

Recall

Q. In the Fundy Settlement case, what decided where the trusts were resident?

A. Where central management and control actually sat. The substantive decisions were made by beneficiaries in Canada, so the trusts were resident in Canada despite an offshore trustee.

Q. What is the danger in going silent too early in a negotiation?

A. Silence is powerful after a clear question, but silence before you have stated your position can let the other side fill the gap with assumptions you will spend the meeting correcting.

Q. What does a sensitivity table in a pro forma show?

A. How a result such as return or value changes when one or two inputs, such as rent or exit cap rate, move up or down. It shows which assumptions the deal is most exposed to.

Why this matters

The vehicle decision lasts as long as the project, and changing it later is usually expensive in tax, legal fees and lender consent. It is also the first meeting where your partners see how you think. If you lead with tax tricks, they will assume you lead with tricks. If you lead with their needs and a clear process, they will trust the structure and you.

The scene

This is a hypothetical scene. A conference room. You, Mr Shabazz, are the developer. Partner One is a local business owner with good income from other businesses who wants to invest equity. Partner Two lives abroad, is investing savings, and wants regular cash. Partner One has brought his accountant. The land is under a conditional agreement. The question on the agenda is "partnership or company?"

Partner One opens: "My accountant says a partnership, because I can use the early losses." Partner Two says: "I don't want to file tax returns in your country every year." The accountant says: "We can make this work for everyone."

The lines to say

  • "Before we pick a vehicle, can we write down three things for each of us: where we are resident, whether we want early losses or regular cash, and how long we expect to stay in?"
  • "Partner Two, when you say you don't want to file here, is it the paperwork, the tax itself, or not knowing what you'll owe?"
  • "I want the partnership agreement, the loan terms and the tax analysis reviewed together before anyone signs."
  • To the accountant: "What would make you uncomfortable signing your name to this analysis?" Then stop talking.
  • "Every rate in this room is provisional until each of our advisers has checked it in writing."

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

  • "It's all tax-free if we put it offshore." It is never all tax-free, land is taxed where it sits, and the sentence tells a careful partner you will cut corners.
  • "Don't worry about the tax side, I'll handle it." You cannot advise them on their own tax, and if it goes wrong it becomes your fault.
  • "My accountant does this all the time." Experience is not analysis, and the other partners need their own adviser.
  • Any rate stated as fact. Say "the accountant's working assumption is" and verify it.

The question behind the question

Partner One's question is not really "partnership or company?" It is "can I use the losses against my other income?" That is a reasonable want, and a flow-through vehicle may serve it. Partner Two's question is not really about tax returns. It is "will I be trapped in a system I don't understand, with withholding I can't recover and bills I can't predict?" The answers to those two questions may pull in different directions, and a good structure can sometimes give each what they need, for example through separate investment routes for resident and non-resident investors, each reviewed by advisers in the relevant countries. The accountant's line, "we can make this work for everyone," is sometimes true and sometimes a sign that one client's interests are leading. The accountant was brought by Partner One.

When to stay silent

After you ask the accountant what would make him uncomfortable, wait. The first answer is usually reassurance. The second, if you give it space, is usually the real caveat: "Well, the loss allocation depends on how the authority views the financing." That sentence is worth the whole meeting. Write it down and make it an action.

Holding your state

The pressure in this room is subtle: everyone wants to leave with a decision, and the land deadline is real. Hold your state by holding the process. Speak more slowly than the room. Keep your three questions on a card in front of you and return to them when the conversation drifts. If you feel the urge to decide today, name it: "I'd like to decide this week, not this hour." A slow, clear voice reads as confidence; a fast answer reads as a sales pitch.

Closing the meeting

Close with actions, not a decision you are not ready to make. A good closing line is: "Here is what I heard. Partner One wants early losses and has other income. Partner Two wants predictable cash and no surprises abroad. I want a vehicle the lender will accept and that we can explain to an auditor. Our accountant will set out two options against those needs by Friday, each of you will have your own adviser review them, and we decide on the following Tuesday." Then ask each partner, by name, whether that is a fair summary. A partner who says "yes" in front of the others has agreed to a process, which is the most valuable thing you can leave with.

If someone pushes to decide now because of the land deadline, separate the two decisions. The land agreement can usually be assigned to, or taken in the name of, a vehicle chosen later, if the agreement permits it. Ask your lawyer whether it does before the meeting, so you can answer the pressure with a fact instead of a feeling.

The biggest risk

Choosing a vehicle that serves the loudest partner and quietly burdens the others, who discover the cost at their first tax filing. The control is a written needs table for every partner, a written tax analysis that addresses each line of it, and each partner's own adviser confirming their position before signing. Professional sign-off required: a corporate lawyer and a tax adviser for the vehicle, and each partner's own tax adviser.

The beginner's mistake

Letting one partner's adviser become everyone's adviser. An adviser owes duties to their client. Make sure every party knows who that is.

Monthly thread: decision journals

Kema asks you to make one entry in your decision journal after this kind of meeting. Write the decision, the options you rejected, the facts you relied on, the tax assumption and who gave it, and what would tell you that you were wrong. Date it, and note where you were when you decided.

The last two items are not decoration. Rule 22 said residence follows the decisions. A journal that records where and by whom decisions were made is a private habit that can become evidence. Keep it honest, because a journal that flatters you is worse than none.

Callback

Week 6 gave you the pattern for hostile questions: acknowledge, bridge, answer. Partner Two's worry is a quiet hostile question, and it deserves the same respect: acknowledge the fear, bridge to the process, and answer with the specific check you will do. Week 3's lesson on incentives applies too: ask whom the accountant works for.

Recap

Ask every partner's residence, needs and horizon before naming a vehicle. Never promise tax-free, never state a rate as fact, never advise others on their own tax. Find the question behind the question, wait for the second answer, and keep your pace slower than the room.

Next: Kema, Quiz and Recap, on how tax works.
checklist: Bring a needs table: residence, losses or cash, and horizon for each partner
Ask the question behind each partner's stated preference
Ask the adviser what would make them uncomfortable signing, then wait
Say every rate is provisional until verified in writing
Never promise tax-free, and never advise a partner on their own tax
Confirm whose client each adviser is
Record the decision, the assumptions and where it was made in your journal
head: Field checklist
speak: The meeting where partners choose a vehicle is really a meeting about what each person needs. Before naming partnership or company, write down three things for each partner: where they are resident, whether they want early losses or regular cash, and how long they expect to stay. Then look for the question behind the question. The partner who wants a partnership is usually asking to use losses against other income. The non-resident who does not want to file is usually afraid of being trapped by withholding and bills he cannot predict. Never say it is all tax-free offshore, never advise a partner on his own tax, and never state a rate as fact. Ask the accountant what would make him uncomfortable signing, then stay silent until the real caveat arrives. Speak slower than the room, and decide this week, not this hour.
terms: Needs table — a written list of each partner's residence, wants and horizon, used before choosing a vehicle
Question behind the question — the underlying concern that a stated preference is really about
Adviser's client — the person to whom an adviser owes duties, which may not be everyone in the room

hostile.q: Your partner's accountant designed this structure. Who was looking after my interests?
hostile.a: Nobody in this room can look after your tax interests except your own adviser, and the agreement makes that a condition before you sign. The analysis addresses your line of the needs table separately, and if your adviser disagrees with it, we revisit the structure before we close, not after.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: How tax works: the week in six questions
summary: Six questions on residence, source, character and flow-through entities, a Red Pen drill on a structure memo with planted defects, and a two-minute boardroom explanation of the week.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week comes down to one habit: answer who taxes, what kind of profit, and through whom, before you go near a rate. Today we test it, mark up a flawed memo, and say the whole week in two minutes.

Recall

Q. Why does the character of a gain change your equity multiple?

A. Because income and capital are often taxed differently. In the hypothetical example, a 1,000,000 gain left 2,800,000 if taxed as capital and 2,600,000 if taxed as income, moving the multiple from 1.4 to 1.3.

Q. What is a remedy for breach of contract?

A. What the law gives the innocent party, most often damages to put them where they would have been had the contract been performed, and sometimes specific performance or termination.

Q. Name two operating expenses a rental pro forma must carry.

A. Property tax and insurance, along with repairs, utilities paid by the owner, management and a reserve for replacements.

Why this matters

Tax will touch every deal you do for the rest of your career, and most of what you need is judgment, not memorised rates. If you can ask these questions quickly and correctly, you will brief advisers better, catch weak structures earlier, and avoid promising things you cannot deliver.

The six questions

Question 1. What is the difference between residence and source taxation? Answer: residence taxation is based on who the taxpayer is and usually reaches worldwide income; source taxation is based on where the income arises and usually reaches only income earned there. Land is taxed heavily on a source basis because it cannot move.

Question 2. Who decides whether a profit is income or capital? Answer: the facts do, as read by the authority and ultimately the courts. Intention at purchase, holding period, frequency of similar deals, financing, and activity such as subdivision and marketing all point one way or the other. The label you choose does not decide it.

Question 3. In the Fundy Settlement case, why did the offshore trustee's address not decide residence? Answer: because the test is where central management and control actually sits, and the substantive decisions were made by beneficiaries in Canada. Rule 22: residence follows the decisions, not the address.

Question 4. What is phantom income, and how do you protect against it? Answer: taxable profit allocated to an owner who received no cash, often because cash went to non-deductible loan principal. Protect against it with a tax distribution clause reconciled with the loan covenants.

Question 5. Why can a hybrid entity be dangerous? Answer: because one country treats it as transparent and another as a separate taxpayer, which can produce double tax, lost credits, or a mismatch that anti-hybrid rules attack.

Question 6. A seller wants 1,000,000 after tax. How do you find the price? Answer: divide the after-tax target by one minus his assumed rate to get the pre-tax gain, then add his tax cost and selling costs. Do it on both the income and capital assumptions, and send him to his own adviser for his actual position.

Say that out loud now.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical memo and find the defects before you read on.

"Structure memo. HoldCo is incorporated abroad and is therefore resident there. The developer will continue to approve all decisions from home for efficiency. The building will be held as an investment, so any gain will be capital. ProjectCo is a partnership, so there will be no tax. The capital gains rate is 15 percent per our accountant. Losses will be allocated entirely to Partner One because he can use them best. Partner Two, who lives abroad, will not need to file anything."

The defects. One: incorporation abroad does not settle residence; central management and control matters, and the next sentence says decisions will be made at home, which undermines the first. Two: calling it an investment does not make the gain capital; the facts at the time will decide. Three: a partnership is flow-through, not tax-free; the partners pay. Four: a rate is stated as fact from a single source; it should be labelled provisional and verified against the primary source for the relevant year. Five: allocating all losses to the partner who can use them, without economic substance behind it, is exactly the kind of allocation authorities may not respect. Six: a non-resident partner's filing and withholding position cannot be assumed; it needs advice in both countries.

The week on one page

QuestionWhat decides itThe trap
Who taxes?Residence of the person, source of the incomeAssuming registration settles residence
What kind of profit?Facts: intention, holding, financing, activityBelieving the label decides it
Through whom?Legal form and tax treatment, separatelyThinking flow-through means tax-free
Is the number right?Rebuilding it from the transaction upGrossing up by adding the rate

Read the table aloud once, row by row. If any row makes you hesitate, go back to that day's lesson tonight. The point of a recap is not to feel finished; it is to find the one idea you cannot yet say cleanly, and fix it while the week is fresh.

Boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes to an investment committee. Set a timer. Then compare with this model answer.

"Before we talk about any rate, we answer three questions. First, who taxes this: the country where the land sits will tax it on a source basis, and the countries where our investors and entities are resident may also tax it, with relief depending on their rules. Second, what kind of profit: the facts decide whether a gain is income or capital, so our acquisition record, financing and conduct will support the character we have modelled, and we will not behave inconsistently with it. Third, through whom: we have compared a flow-through vehicle with a company. The partnership gives early losses to the investors who can use them, but it creates phantom income when cash repays principal, so the agreement has a tax distribution clause reconciled with the loan. Every entity will be managed where it is resident, with minutes that prove it. All rates in the model are provisional and are being verified by advisers in each country."

Scoring your boardroom answer

Score yourself 1 to 5 on four things. Accuracy: did you say anything you could not defend, especially a rate stated as fact? Structure: did you give the three questions in order, or wander? Composure: did your pace stay steady when you reached the hard part, the phantom income? The hard question: did you name the risk before anyone asked, or hope nobody would? A 3 on every line is a good first attempt. Record it on your phone, listen once, and do it again tomorrow without notes.

The biggest risk

Thinking this week's ideas are the adviser's job. The adviser answers questions; you must know which questions to ask. The control is to bring the three questions, in order, to every structuring conversation, and to require written advice from a qualified tax adviser in each relevant country.

The beginner's mistake

Memorising rates instead of questions. Rates change with every budget. The questions do not.

Callback

In week 14 you built a pro forma to a stabilised net operating income. This week showed that NOI is the start of the tax story, not the end: interest, depreciation, principal and character all stand between NOI and what an owner keeps. And in week 20, the contract decided what binds. This week the contract decided who pays the tax.

Recap

Residence versus source, income versus capital, flow-through versus separate taxpayer. Residence follows decisions. Character follows facts. Flow-through moves tax to owners, sometimes without cash. Work backward from outcomes to check them. Lead with needs in the room.

head: The six questions
speak: This week, one habit: before any rate, answer who taxes, what kind of profit, and through whom. The country where the land sits taxes on a source basis, and the countries where people and entities are resident may tax too. Residence follows the decisions, not the address, as the Fundy Settlement case showed. Whether a gain is income or capital depends on the facts, not the label: intention, holding period, financing and activity. A flow-through vehicle moves the tax to the owners, and when cash goes to repay principal, they can be taxed on profit they never received, so add a tax distribution clause and check it against the loan. Watch for hybrid entities treated differently in two countries. When you meet a number, work backward to the transaction and test it. And in the room, ask each partner's needs before naming a vehicle. Rates come last, verified.
terms: Source taxation — taxation by the country where income arises, which for land is almost always the country where it sits
Character — whether a profit is business income or a capital gain, decided by the facts
Information return — a filing made by a flow-through entity that reports profit and each owner's share without paying the tax itself

hostile.q: Why should we believe your gain will be taxed as capital when you're a developer?
hostile.a: You shouldn't take my word for it. The acquisition resolution records an intention to hold, the financing is long-term, we have no history of selling this kind of asset quickly, and the model shows the result if the gain is taxed as income instead. A qualified adviser has reviewed the facts in writing. If our conduct changes, so will the assumption, and we will tell you.
